paragraphs: BEIJING, Nov 16 (Reuters) - At a top private school in Beijing, 13-year-old Peng Gaodi has used artificial intelligence to build more than 200 apps, including a homework-submission platform and a secondhand marketplace. He pitches ideas to real investors, idolises Elon Musk and hopes to become a computer scientist.

Around him, classmates program humanoid robots to play soccer, attend coding workshops and train on flight simulators. Posters across the 30-acre (12-hectare) boarding school campus encourage students to "create a virtual world in five minutes with AI vibe coding."

"In the past, if I couldn't solve a problem at home, I'd have to call my teacher, which increases their workload," Peng said. "But now I can just ask AI to help me learn better. It noticeably improved my learning efficiency."

Rare access granted to Reuters at the $39,000-a-year Beijing New Talent Academy offered a window into China's push to weave AI into education. The school, which serves more than 2,000 students, has built its own digital innovation curriculum covering AI, robotics and programming, and developed a classroom AI model incorporating features from popular Chinese systems.

The academy represents the sharp end of a broader transformation. With almost 200 million students enrolled in primary and secondary education, China is undertaking one of the world's largest AI-assisted learning experiments, with the technology increasingly integrated into teaching nationwide.

By 2030, Beijing wants AI literacy to be universal among schoolchildren. Current broad AI education guidelines state that students should progress from understanding basic concepts in their early years to applying advanced tools and critical-thinking skills in complex projects.

A weeks-long Reuters examination, based on school visits, interviews with more than a dozen educators, parents and experts, and a review of more than 100 academic papers and government procurement records, paints one of the most detailed pictures yet of how AI is reshaping Chinese classrooms. It found a sweeping but uneven effort to build a generation of AI-savvy innovators, with little consensus on what AI literacy means, how it should be taught or measured.

China views the technology as central to its economic future and technological rivalry with the United States, hoping early exposure will nurture the homegrown innovation needed for major breakthroughs.

Beijing's state-led push far outpaces efforts in the West. President Xi Jinping has declared AI education fundamental to reform. By contrast, the US relies on decentralized, nonbinding guidance and lacks dedicated funding or state-level teacher standards, according to Stanford University's 2026 AI Index.

A Reuters review of provincial "AI+ education" blueprints reveals a degree of official coordination unseen elsewhere. Nearly half of China's provinces and municipalities have rolled out binding plans. Shanghai mandates at least 30 hours of annual teaching on AI skills per grade, while the Beijing city government plans to integrate AI into student health monitoring, as well as set up 100 AI pilot demonstration schools. Underscoring its importance, regions including Ningxia and Gansu plan to integrate AI literacy directly into high-stakes school entrance exams by 2027.

The documents also offer an early look at more expansive classroom applications. Beyond coding and tutoring, Guizhou is integrating AI facial recognition and behavioral analysis into classrooms, while Shanghai is deploying systems for mental and physical health monitoring. In Yunnan, 14,000 classrooms are slated to have lessons recorded and analysed by AI, turning Chinese schools into a high-stakes testing ground for the opportunities and risks confronting global education.
As AI spreads through Chinese classrooms, many educators are grappling with how to deploy the technology without reinforcing the rote-learning habits policymakers want to move beyond.

Reuters found starkly different approaches across the country. While some schools encourage students like Peng to build and create with AI, others are focused on using the technology to plug gaps in educational resources.

"Implementation is all over the place," said Ted Mo Chen, chief of staff at Chinese education technology startup ClassIn, adding that few schools he had visited had integrated AI into the curriculum effectively.
China's education ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
CLASSROOMS OF THE FUTURE

Headmaster Liu Wei said only a small minority of students at Beijing New Talent Academy would become AI scientists or engineers. For the rest, the objective is to make AI an everyday tool for learning and creating.

Hundreds of kilometres away in rural Anhui province, Funan County Qinqing High School is using the same technology to solve a problem affluent urban areas in China rarely face: a shortage of qualified teachers.

The school's 4,000 pupils, most of them children of migrant workers, learn core subjects through AI-generated lessons, according to headmaster Yang Tianliang. Students follow personalised classes on tablets, with AI agents posing questions rather than providing answers when they struggle.
"An AI agent doesn't suffer from fatigue, and it never makes a student feel stupid for asking a basic question," Yang said.

The school uses popular Chinese AI models from Alibaba's Qwen, ByteDance and Z.AI to generate text, images, interactive lessons and videos. Yang said it had also introduced small-group projects to encourage greater student interaction.

He credited the approach with helping lift university admission rates from below 60% to 90% in recent years, although Reuters could not independently verify the figures. Yang estimated at least 200 other Chinese schools were experimenting with similar systems.
An Alibaba spokesperson said its open-source AI models and Cloud for Youth Programme give students direct access to AI tools and education. ByteDance and Z.AI did not respond to requests for comment.
Schools such as Funan County Qinqing High School offer a glimpse of how quickly AI is spreading through China's education system.

Since 2024, China's education ministry has encouraged schools to introduce AI courses, train teachers and develop pilot programmes. Primary-school pupils are introduced to basic AI tools, while older students learn how AI systems work and apply them to increasingly sophisticated projects.
A Reuters review of more than 100 government procurement documents found authorities committed at least $31 million in the past year to AI classroom equipment, training and teaching platforms.

The true figure is likely far higher, scattered across thousands of local budgets and not officially tallied. Consultancy iResearch estimates 2025 spending on education digitalisation at just under $83 billion, with generative AI projects accounting for 46% of AI education procurement.
AN EXPERIMENT WITHOUT A CLEAR SCORECARD
China has yet to establish a standard framework for measuring AI literacy, leaving schools to experiment and making success difficult to assess.
"Mature, widely adopted assessment rubrics for compulsory school-level AI competency are still being built," said Selena Guo, portfolio lead at research firm China Policy.

Preliminary research into AI's effects on children's learning also offers mixed signals, with some studies suggesting short-term gains while raising questions about longer-term intellectual development.

A recent study examining nearly 27,000 Chinese teenagers found AI adoption was associated with an 18% increase in homework scores but a 20% decline in monthly examination scores within six months, with the biggest declines in social science subjects.

Another nationwide Chinese survey this year involving more than 320,000 pupils reported educational benefits from AI but also concerns about dependence and weaker independent thinking. Students using AI at least three times weekly showed lower memory, comprehension, analytical and creative skills than less frequent users.

The findings do not establish causation but reinforce teacher concerns about cognitive outsourcing, where children increasingly delegate mental tasks to technology rather than develop those skills themselves.
Chen from ClassIn warned that children's thinking processes could be "completely bypassed" if schools failed to prevent them from relying on AI for quick answers.
Chinese academic research reviewed by Reuters also suggested that students in rural areas may be particularly vulnerable to cognitive outsourcing and device addiction.
FINDING THE RIGHT BALANCE
Some educators and parents are already experimenting with safeguards to keep AI from replacing critical thinking.

At Beijing New Talent Academy, Peng said he tries to solve coding problems himself before asking AI for hints rather than complete answers. He said the technology has helped deepen his understanding of maths.
"I think AI is a tool that helps me, not something I depend on."
For Beijing parent Rita Luan, whose 11-year-old daughter attends a leading public school in the capital, the challenge is ensuring that AI strengthens rather than shortcuts learning.

She said her daughter's school still largely teaches AI concepts rather than practical applications, so she supplements lessons at home, teaching her daughter to prompt ByteDance's Doubao chatbot under close supervision.
Her rule: spend 15 minutes trying to solve a difficult maths problem before turning to AI. Days later, Luan asks her to solve the same problem without help.
"The point is to make sure she actually digested the solution," she said.

paragraphs: U.S. District Judge Jessica Clarke granted a judgment of acquittal for Anton Peraire-Bueno and James Peraire-Bueno on November 16, 2026, ending a prosecution that tested whether exploiting vulnerabilities in decentralized blockchain trading infrastructure could constitute criminal fraud.

The decision follows a November 2025 mistrial, when jurors could not reach a unanimous verdict after nearly four weeks of testimony. Prosecutors subsequently sought another trial, but Clarke concluded that the evidence presented could not legally support convictions for wire fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud or conspiracy to commit money laundering.
The central issue was whether the brothers made materially false representations when executing a trading strategy that exploited Ethereum‘s transaction-ordering infrastructure.

Prosecutors alleged that the brothers manipulated the system used to construct and validate Ethereum transactions, allowing them to intercept private trading information and replace transactions submitted by automated trading bots.
Clarke concluded that the government had not demonstrated that the brothers made a legally actionable misrepresentation during the operation.

The judge examined whether registering a validator, requesting transaction blocks, submitting invalid block information or proposing modified transactions constituted deceptive representations. She found that none of those actions established the necessary element of wire fraud.
The ruling also rejected the argument that violating the intended design of the MEV-Boost system was sufficient to establish criminal deception.
The judge distinguished between potentially objectionable trading behavior and conduct prohibited by the specific criminal statutes under which the brothers were charged.
Because the money laundering conspiracy charge depended on the proceeds of the alleged wire fraud, the failure of the underlying fraud case also required acquittal on that charge.

As FinanceFeeds previously reported, prosecutors had challenged efforts by the DeFi Education Fund to submit arguments concerning the wider implications of criminalizing blockchain trading strategies.

The ruling limits the government’s ability to prosecute this particular blockchain exploit under traditional wire fraud provisions without evidence of material deception. However, the decision does not establish that exploiting software vulnerabilities is universally lawful or prevent enforcement under other applicable statutes.
The case originated from an April 2023 operation involving maximal extractable value, or MEV, a mechanism through which traders and validators can profit from the ordering of blockchain transactions.

Ethereum validators are responsible for proposing transaction blocks, while specialized builders assemble transactions to maximize potential returns. MEV-Boost, open-source software introduced by Flashbots, allows validators to outsource block construction through intermediaries known as relays.

Prosecutors alleged that the Peraire-Bueno brothers identified a vulnerability in this arrangement and developed a strategy called Omakase to target automated traders conducting sandwich transactions.
Sandwich trading involves placing transactions immediately before and after another trader’s order to profit from changes in the asset’s price.

According to the trial evidence, the brothers created transactions designed to attract these automated strategies. They then exploited a relay vulnerability to access transaction information that the bots expected to remain private before submitting replacement transactions.
The operation generated approximately $25 million in profits within a single Ethereum block.

The brothers were indicted in May 2024. Prosecutors maintained that the operation amounted to fraud, while defense lawyers argued that their clients had executed a trading strategy without making false representations or violating applicable trading rules.
Following the deadlocked jury, prosecutors requested a retrial for early 2026. The defense instead pursued a judgment of acquittal, which Clarke ultimately granted.

The case demonstrates that technical vulnerabilities in transaction-ordering systems can expose sophisticated trading operations to substantial losses. For institutional DeFi participants, protections around private transaction information and relay infrastructure remain important regardless of whether a particular exploit meets the legal definition of fraud.
The decision adds to a series of federal court rulings examining whether unconventional decentralized trading strategies can be prosecuted under existing financial fraud statutes.

In May 2025, another Manhattan federal judge overturned fraud and market manipulation convictions against Mango Markets trader Avraham Eisenberg, whose trading strategy extracted approximately $110 million from the Solana-based decentralized finance platform.
That ruling involved separate questions concerning jurisdiction, market rules and whether the defendant’s transactions amounted to fraudulent representations.
Clarke’s decision likewise focused on the legal requirements for proving deception rather than determining whether the trading strategy was commercially acceptable.

The similarities do not make the cases interchangeable. Both decisions arose from their particular facts, charges and trial records, and neither creates a general exemption for blockchain manipulation.

The November 16 judgment closes the criminal case against the Peraire-Bueno brothers in the Southern District of New York, eliminating the retrial prosecutors had previously sought.
The decision may also inform future arguments about how fraud statutes apply to automated trading, transaction ordering and decentralized market infrastructure.

For prosecutors, the ruling demonstrates the importance of identifying specific deceptive conduct rather than relying solely on evidence that a trading strategy violated a system’s expected operation.

For blockchain developers, exchanges and institutional trading firms, the distinction between software specifications, enforceable contractual obligations and criminal law remains central to assessing operational and legal risk.

The acquittal removes immediate criminal exposure for the two defendants but leaves broader questions about MEV-related market conduct unresolved. Institutional participants still need to assess smart-contract security, counterparty exposure and the legal treatment of their trading activities independently of this ruling.

paragraphs: Nov 16 (Reuters) - The US Department of Justice will review DoorDash's proposed acquisition of Instacart, according to two people familiar with the matter, bringing antitrust scrutiny to the multibillion-dollar grocery delivery tie-up.
DoorDash said in October it would buy Instacart in a deal valued at about $17 billion to create a dominant platform for ordering food and household essentials online.

"We can affirm that the Department under President (Donald) Trump's leadership will vigorously enforce antitrust laws across industries," a DOJ spokesperson said, declining to confirm the review of the specific merger.
Spokespeople for the two companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Large mergers and acquisitions in the US are required to undergo review by either the DOJ or the Federal Trade Commission, which have historically split scrutiny based on industry expertise.
But if a deal poses competition problems, authorities can negotiate settlements requiring the sale of assets to competitors, or they can sue in federal court to block it.
DoorDash has agreed to pay Instacart $1.25 billion if the deal does not clear antitrust scrutiny, according to a securities filing.
Among standalone delivery apps, Instacart competes with DoorDash and Uber Eats, both of which have been aggressively expanding into grocery and other retail delivery.
Instacart last year announced a partnership with Grubhub, another food delivery platform, to expand restaurant choices on its app and tap into suburban markets.
DoorDash has touted its lead in grocery and retail, saying in February that it had more of those orders than Instacart.

paragraphs: WASHINGTON, Nov 16 (Reuters) - The US Commerce Department and Justice Department released information on Sunday about an investigation into Singapore-based company Megaspeed, saying the probe began in 2024.

Megaspeed has come under scrutiny after reports that Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang stepped down following an investigation that found a Singaporean executive at the company, Alice Huang, had ties to Chinese intelligence.
Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on November 12 and Reuters has not been able to reach him for comment. Alice Huang has denied the allegations.

"After identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential export control violations, the Department of Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024," the Commerce Department and Justice Department said in a joint statement.
In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia about its dealings with Megaspeed, according to the statement.

US agents, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted search operations at multiple locations associated with Megaspeed in Singapore, and at an affiliated data centre site in Newark, California, the statement said.
Following the enforcement action, the Justice Department took the lead role in a criminal investigation with support from the Department of Commerce, it said.
The statement said that while US agencies typically did not comment on ongoing investigations, they were doing so now to provide clarity and to prevent the spread of inaccurate information.
US AND SINGAPORE DISCUSSIONS ON MEGASPEED
Megaspeed said on Sunday that Alice Huang officially left the company on August 31, 2025, but was suspended as chief executive officer on July 10, 2025.
Singapore's government said on Monday it had agreed to continue discussions with the US after Washington released the details of its Megaspeed investigation.
It said last week that Alice Huang had previously worked as the company's chief marketing officer, and then as chief executive officer, before stepping down in August 2025.
Police found insufficient evidence that she had committed offenses relating to spying or the theft of trade secrets, it said.
The city-state has barred her from re-entering Singapore, while investigations into Megaspeed and its dealings continue, the Singapore government said.
Several news organizations, including the New York Times, have reported that US intelligence agencies concluded Alice Huang had links to the Chinese government.
Reuters has not been able to verify any of the allegations made in the New York Times or other reports.
US intelligence agencies are still trying to determine her relationship with Chinese intelligence, according to two people briefed on the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Evidence gathered so far indicated she was probably an intelligence asset, someone who provides information to an intelligence service, rather than a trained intelligence officer, they said.
Beijing has rejected allegations that Alice Huang is a spy.

https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacif.title: SK hynix sets $1 billion chip-supplier support plan
https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacif.author: Reuters
paragraphs: SEOUL, Nov 16 (Reuters) - South Korea's SK Hynix said on Monday it plans to spend 1.4 trillion won ($1.05 billion) over the next five years to support domestic suppliers of semiconductor materials, parts and equipment, aiming to strengthen its supply chain as competition intensifies in the AI chip market.

The chipmaker also outlined plans for a jointly funded 874.6 billion won testing facility at its semiconductor complex in Yongin, south of Seoul, where smaller suppliers will be able to test products under conditions similar to those on commercial chip production lines.
Here are some details:

• SK Hynix said its supplier support programme covers four stages - research and development, testing, mass production and sales. It aims to help smaller companies overcome financing and technology hurdles.

• The testing facility, named Trinity Fab, is a partnership between SK Hynix, the central government and local governments. It is scheduled to open in May 2027. SK Hynix will contribute 443.2 billion won, the central government 373.6 billion won and local governments 57.7 billion won, according to the company.
• Trinity Fab will house around 50 semiconductor tools, including lithography and etching equipment, allowing suppliers to test materials and components on 12-inch wafers.
• To reduce financial risks for suppliers, SK Hynix said it will share development costs in advance and provide compensation if a joint project fails.
• An independent foundation will operate the test facility to protect the intellectual property of participating suppliers, the company said.
• The initiative also includes establishing an overseas marketing support centre to help domestic suppliers expand internationally and reduce reliance on imported chip components.

• SK Hynix and financial institutions will also provide 2 trillion won in financing backed by the Korea Trade Insurance Corporation, while other programmes offer low-interest loans and technical consulting to suppliers, including smaller subcontractors.

https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospa.title: Rocket from Boeing-Lockheed firm fails mid-flight, destroys payload of Amazon satellites
https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospa.author: Reuters
paragraphs: Nov 15 (Reuters) - A Vulcan rocket owned by United Launch Alliance, the joint venture of Boeing and Lockheed Martin, failed on Sunday shortly after liftoff from Florida, destroying its payload of 40 satellites from Amazon's Leo internet network in the launch company's first mission failure.

The rocket failed roughly 10 minutes after liftoff from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, and the cause was not immediately clear. It represented a major setback for the two-decade-old company's new flagship rocket as ULA sought to begin a regular cadence of launches for Amazon's burgeoning satellite internet constellation.

"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in a statement.
"Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don't have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today," ULA said.

The failure is expected to lead to a lengthy technical investigation that would keep the rocket off the market for months. This could deepen a US launch bottleneck brought on by other rocket mishaps and challenges across the industry as well as the looming retirement of SpaceX's Falcon 9, the world's most active rocket. SpaceX is no longer accepting bookings for the Falcon 9.

"There is risk with any launch, and that's especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01," Amazon said in a statement, referring to the name of Sunday's mission. "ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they'll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan."

The Sunday flight was Vulcan's fifth since its 2024 debut and first in nine months, following a launch hiatus drawn out by separate technical investigations into its solid rocket side boosters and its core BE-4 engines, which are supplied by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin space company.
Blue Origin is working with ULA in the investigation into Sunday's failure, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The boosters were being scrutinized for issues encountered on Vulcan's last two flights, including a mission in February for the US Space Force. Both missions successfully delivered their payloads to orbit, but the Pentagon had not yet approved the rocket to resume flying national security payloads, pending its performance with the Amazon mission on Sunday.

Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket with the BE-4 engine had a launchpad explosion in May, and its investigation determined the engine was the cause. That led the company to modify those delivered to ULA for Vulcan, ULA spokesperson Jessica Rye told Reuters in August.

It was unclear if the BE-4 engines played a role in Sunday's mission failure. It appeared to occur after the separation of Vulcan's second stage, the portion carrying the Amazon satellites, from the first-stage booster powered by the BE-4 engines.

ULA was formed in 2006 in a merger of Boeing's Delta rocket program and Lockheed Martin's Atlas rocket program. The company had embraced what was a 100% mission success record ever since. Its Delta and Atlas rockets had only suffered a handful of failures in the decades before the merger.
AMAZON'S ELUSIVE ACCESS TO SPACE

The failure is another setback for Amazon as it races to deploy satellites using third-party launch providers, many of which have had groundings and failures. The New Glenn explosion in May happened days before it was due to launch Amazon Leo satellites.
The rocket failures have persistently held up Amazon's bid to rival SpaceX's vast Starlink internet network, which has more than 11,000 satellites and millions of customers worldwide.
SpaceX's wide lead over its satellite rivals is due in part to the advantage of having its own rocket to launch its satellites, while other companies spend billions of dollars on external launches.

Since 2025, 398 Leo satellites have been deployed across 14 launches, about 12% of the 3,236 satellites Amazon needs for global service coverage. The company has hoped to start initial internet service this year.

https://www.reuters.com/world/china/chin.title: China taps US AI models to train homegrown rivals as chip curbs bite
https://www.reuters.com/world/china/chin.author: Reuters
paragraphs: Chinese entities are adopting increasingly sophisticated ways to use output from leading American AI models to train domestic competitors, as Beijing seeks workarounds to tightening US curbs on advanced chips.

A Reuters review of more than 300 Chinese academic papers, patents, corporate disclosures, recruitment notices and government documents from the past year revealed the scale of the practice, which has moved from the laboratory to mainstream industrial use.

The records describe Chinese researchers using US models to produce answers to questions, build computer code and find solutions to complex problems, and using that output to teach and train domestic rivals.
The documents also show that Beijing is encouraging distillation to make AI cheaper and easier to deploy across China's massive manufacturing sector.

Distillation is not illegal and is prevalent in other parts of the world. While the process cannot reproduce a leading model's full capabilities or entirely replace heavy computing power, it helps developers retain important skills in smaller, cheaper systems.
China's broadening use of distillation could undercut the effectiveness of US curbs on the sale of advanced semiconductors, especially graphics processing units (GPUs) made by US chip giant Nvidia.
Distillation is also a source of friction between the world's two biggest economies ahead of the November 19-20 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen.
US authorities publicly accused Chinese companies in September of aggressive, targeted distillation of US models to bridge Beijing's computing power gap.

And at meetings in Chengdu in July, US Commerce Department officials raised concerns with Chinese regulators and tech executives about companies in China distilling American models, two people familiar with the discussions said.
Chinese officials defended distillation as a standard AI-development technique and said they were open to discussing the issue, one person said.
The US Commerce Department and China's Cyberspace Administration did not respond to requests for comment.

Distillation involves a powerful 'teacher' model generating answers or demonstrating how to complete a task, while a smaller 'student' model learns to mimic the teacher's outputs and reasoning processes.

For Chinese developers facing constraints on computing power, the attraction is in making one expensive request to a foreign model to produce data that can then train domestic models multiple times at much lower cost.

In a November 2024 paper, Shanghai Jiao Tong University researchers described selecting about 5,000 questions answered by OpenAI's GPT-4o, converting the answers into data points, and using them to train a domestic model for complex reasoning.
The researchers also cautioned that excessive reliance on distillation could stifle original innovation, writing that it "might result in the model learning to mimic rather than truly understand".
The project illustrated how American model output can become reusable data, allowing developers to improve capabilities while spending far less on training.

Alibaba researchers described a more systematic approach in an April 2025 paper, using OpenAI's GPT-4o to generate answers for training data, and then deploying a verification system to check the quality of that data.

In a February 2026 paper, researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Chinese food-delivery giant Meituan wrote of using GPT-4o and Anthropic's Claude 3.5 Sonnet to train a multi-modal model to handle complex visual and textual information.
Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Alibaba and Meituan did not respond to requests for comment.

Among leading American AI companies, OpenAI's terms restrict using its output to develop competing models. Anthropic's terms say outputs cannot be used to create products that compete with its services.
A US official familiar with the July Chengdu regulatory discussions said Washington believes industrial distillation of American models on this scale goes beyond normal developer activity.

Two people familiar with Chinese developers' operations disputed that assessment, saying distillation is common practice across the global AI industry and that developers follow international standards.
Chinese government documents do not instruct companies to distil American models but encourage distillation to make AI technology affordable and scalable for manufacturing and services.
A national AI+Manufacturing policy package published by eight Chinese government agencies in January explicitly prioritised using distillation to develop lightweight, industry-specific AI models.
The policies reflect Beijing's ambition to deploy smaller, cheaper AI systems across industries.
Concerned by distillation's growing geopolitical sensitivities, Chinese AI developers have in recent months asked Beijing to provide clearer guidance on the practice.
China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology did not respond to a request for comment.

Germany’s government plans to buy RWE and E.ON’s one-third stake in uranium enrichment company Urenco for up to €4 billion, German newspapers reported, in a deal Britain requested to keep the stake in European hands as it prepares to use Urenco to make fuel for its military reactors, including those powering its nuclear submarines.

Die Welt first reported on Thursday evening that a new line had appeared in the Bundestag’s final deliberations on the 2027 draft budget, setting aside €4 billion for “the acquisition and holding of stakes in companies in the energy sector.” Political sources told the paper the money was apparently earmarked for Urenco. The finance and economy ministries declined to say what the line was for.

Handelsblatt, citing government circles, said London asked Berlin to buy the stake so it would not go to another buyer, and that Urenco is set to play a central role in modernizing Britain’s nuclear deterrent.

Urenco is owned in equal thirds by the British government, the Dutch government and a holding company jointly owned by E.ON and RWE. It runs enrichment plants in Gronau in Germany, Almelo in the Netherlands, Capenhurst in England and Eunice, New Mexico, the only commercial enrichment facility operating in the United States. Gronau is Germany’s only uranium enrichment plant and was exempted from the country’s nuclear phase-out with an indefinite operating permit.

Berlin has confirmed it was told of Britain’s plans to make reactor fuel for defence purposes, which it says complies with the 1970 Treaty of Almelo that founded Urenco and limits it to civilian work.

According to Welt, the stake lost its strategic value for both utilities when Germany phased out nuclear power, and Urenco’s growing military work has made them uneasy. RWE has said it wants to sell its minority stake, and E.ON chief executive Leonhard Birnbaum has said a sale would need the government’s approval, Reuters reported.

The stake has been hard to sell previously. When it was last up for sale in 2016, Börsen-Zeitung reported that Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom and France’s Areva had shown interest, which was denied, and that the Treaty of Almelo required Berlin to be consulted on any sale.
The government and both companies declined to comment. E.ON shares rose 1.5% on Friday, among the biggest gainers on the DAX, and RWE gained 0.3%.

BRUSSELS, Nov 17 (Reuters) - The European Union tech regulator charged Chinese e-commerce giant Temu on Tuesday for not doing enough to stop the sale of illegal products on its platform in breach of online content rules, putting it at risk of a second hefty fine.

The European Commission, which acts as the tech regulator for the 27-country bloc, said Temu's mitigation measures "include ineffective controls to check the compliance of products; a weak content moderation system; and an ineffective sanction system".

A spokesperson for Temu said the company disagreed with the Commission's preliminary findings and that the company makes significant efforts to mitigate illegal product risk. The e-commerce giant will respond to the Commission, he said.
"We are confident that we will reach an amicable resolution of the matter that fully addresses the Commission's remaining concerns," the spokesperson said.
The Commission said that Temu, which is owned by PDD Holdings, has the possibility to exercise its rights to defence and reply to its preliminary findings.
If the Commission's findings were ultimately confirmed, it would adopt a "non-compliance decision", which would trigger a fine of up to 6% of the company's annual worldwide turnover.

Such a fine would be the second imposed on Temu, after a €200 million ($220.12 million) penalty in May in the first part of an investigation opened two years ago under the Digital Services Act that requires large online companies to do more to tackle illegal and harmful content on their platforms.
The earlier fine was for not assessing the risks of sales of illegal products, while Tuesday's charges were for not taking adequate measures to stop such sales.
The Commission said last month it had accepted Temu's action plan to remedy the breach that had triggered the existing fine.

Temu, along with Shein and other e-commerce platforms, has also been hit by the EU imposing €3 fees on low-value e-commerce packages since the start of July. Parcels worth less than €150 previously entered the bloc duty-free.

paragraphs: WASHINGTON, Nov 17 (Reuters) - The Trump administration plans to press ahead with efforts to block imports of Chinese data center equipment despite pushback from Amazon, Google, Meta and other US technology companies, people briefed on the matter said.

Reuters reported in August that the Federal Communications Commission was seeking to ban US imports of new models of Chinese optical transceivers, which allow data to travel over fiber-optic cables at the speed of light within data centers, over national security concerns.

But the measure has faced more opposition than was previously known, with Amazon, Google, Meta, CoreWeave and Cisco joining Microsoft in a meeting with White House officials earlier this year previously reported by Reuters. US firms could need up to a decade to comply with any such mandate, the executives told the officials, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The lobbying had raised doubts over whether the measure would go ahead. But it is moving forward, three additional people familiar with the matter said, emphasizing that it could still get shelved if sentiment within the administration changes.
Shares of US optical transceiver makers rose after the news, with Coherent up 2.2% and Lumentum up 1.5%.

The momentum is thanks in part to revelations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which have fueled renewed calls in Washington for a tougher stance against Chinese technology threats.

The FCC, Amazon, Google, Meta, CoreWeave and Cisco did not respond to requests for comment. Microsoft declined to comment. A White House official declined to comment on the lobbying or the measure's progress but said recent FCC actions barring Chinese technology and other foreign equipment have resulted in billions in investments into US manufacturing, and thousands of new American jobs.

The Chinese Embassy in Washington said Beijing "firmly opposes the US overstretching the concept of national security" and urges the Trump administration to "stop smearing Chinese companies and threatening them with sanctions."
"China will continue to do what is necessary to firmly defend the legitimate and lawful rights and interests of Chinese companies," it added.
China hawks in Washington are concerned Chinese transceivers could be used by Beijing to steal data, install malware or disrupt service at US data centers.

China boasts two-thirds of the global market for optical transceivers, according to Counterpoint Research. Chinese firms like Eoptolink and Zhongji Innolight, which was added to the Pentagon's list of Chinese military-backed companies, dominate global supply, counting top American hyperscalers among their customers.
US-based Coherent and Lumentum produce technology that competes with them but lack the scale to replace Chinese vendors, according to a report by the Foundation for American Innovation.

One of the people said the US firms raised the prospect of retaliation from China, in the form of a ban on the export of indium phosphide, a critical mineral needed for US firms to produce their own optical transceivers.
Trump has taken a more dovish approach to China in his second term, as he faces down Beijing's export controls on rare-earth minerals, which underpin tech manufacturing everywhere.
But the FCC has been a notable exception, successfully barring imports of new models of Chinese drones, robots, power inverters and routers over the last year.
The Huang revelations have added to the pressure on the administration by turning a spotlight on cases of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled to China that went unaddressed by the Commerce Department.

paragraphs: Italy's data protection authority said on Saturday it had fined Facebook's parent company Meta €805 million ($887 million) for accessing Android users' photos and videos without their explicit consent.
The fine concerns a feature on Facebook, available since 2023, which suggests photos and videos from a smartphone's gallery for users to post online.
The feature relied on a single, general permission covering several app functions, and allowed the app to access a smartphone's entire photo archive, including metadata, in most cases permanently.
The regulator said Meta had failed to adequately inform users about the feature or to obtain effective consent. It said about 20 million Android users in Italy were affected.
The €805 million fine corresponds to around 0.47% of the group's global revenue in 2024, according to the authority.
The regulator said it had launched an investigation in July 2025 after a tip-off from the consumer protection centre in Bolzano.

Meta had questioned the Italian authority's jurisdiction in the case and pointed to the data protection authority in Ireland, where the group has its European headquarters. The Italian regulator rejected the objection.
Meta now has 60 days to obtain users' explicit consent to access their photo galleries. It must also switch off the feature as a default, including for users who have already granted general access.

paragraphs: Prosecutors accuse Huawei of scheming to defraud HSBC and other banks about its business in Iran and conspiring to steal trade secrets from five US tech companies. It was also indicted as a criminal enterprise.

“They began with guilt and worked backwards,” defense lawyer Brian Heberlig told jurors in Brooklyn federal court in his closing argument. “When the evidence didn’t fit its theory, it moved the goal posts,” he said.
The government offered jurors a very different picture of the company on Monday, and said prosecutors proved beyond a reasonable doubt that Huawei operated as a criminal enterprise.

“For 20 years, Huawei committed a pattern of crimes targeted at American companies, the American financial system and the American government,” prosecutor Meredith Arfa said in her closing statement. “It is time to finally hold Huawei accountable,” Arfa said.
However, Heberlig argued the banks all knew Huawei operated in Iran, which is under US sanctions. He said the banks accepted the risk and competed for Huawei’s business.
In relation to the alleged theft of trade secrets, “the government cherry-picked a handful of incidents … and tried to convert them into a 20-year conspiracy,” Heberlig said.
“Huawei didn’t steal its way to success,” he said. “It earned it, plain and simple,” he added.
The Huawei case burst into the headlines in 2018 when Meng Wanzhou, its CFO and daughter of the founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant for her role in the alleged bank fraud.
She entered into an agreement with prosecutors in 2021 and the charges against her were dismissed, but the case dragged on.
The jury is likely to begin deliberations on Wednesday. The case went to trial in September. The prosecution put on over 60 witnesses, and the defence about 15.
The jury will deliver its verdict as US-China tensions heat up in the battle over artificial intelligence and amid a fragile trade truce between the two countries.

“They began with guilt and worked backwards,” defense lawyer Brian Heberlig told jurors in Brooklyn federal court in his closing argument. “When the evidence didn’t fit its theory, it moved the goal posts,” he said.

The government offered jurors a very different picture of the company on Monday, and said prosecutors proved beyond a reasonable doubt that Huawei operated as a criminal enterprise.

“For 20 years, Huawei committed a pattern of crimes targeted at American companies, the American financial system and the American government,” prosecutor Meredith Arfa said in her closing statement. “It is time to finally hold Huawei accountable,” Arfa said.

However, Heberlig argued the banks all knew Huawei operated in Iran, which is under US sanctions. He said the banks accepted the risk and competed for Huawei’s business.

In relation to the alleged theft of trade secrets, “the government cherry-picked a handful of incidents … and tried to convert them into a 20-year conspiracy,” Heberlig said.

“Huawei didn’t steal its way to success,” he said. “It earned it, plain and simple,” he added.

The Huawei case burst into the headlines in 2018 when Meng Wanzhou, its CFO and daughter of the founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant for her role in the alleged bank fraud.

The jury will deliver its verdict as US-China tensions heat up in the battle over artificial intelligence and amid a fragile trade truce between the two countries.

Nov 18 : Cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks raised its annual revenue forecast and signed a deal to acquire AI startup Applied Compute in a deal valued at $4.5 billion, as a heightened threat environment pushes customers toward broader security products.
Shares of Palo Alto jumped about 10 per cent in after-hours trading to $368.60, and drove gains in rivals. CrowdStrike rose 5.3 per cent, Zscaler climbed 3 per cent and Fortinet gained 2.1 per cent.

Palo Alto Networks has been repositioning itself as an integrated cybersecurity provider, with recent deals, including its $3.35 billion acquisition of cloud management and monitoring firm Chronosphere and an agreement with Israeli startup Koi.
The company is looking to tap growing cybersecurity spending as the rapid adoption of AI creates new security risks, giving attackers new ways to exploit vulnerabilities.

"As AI accelerates cyber attacks, enterprises are moving with urgency to replace disjointed tools with unified platforms," Palo Alto CEO Nikesh Arora said during the company's analyst call on Wednesday.
With the acquisition of Applied Compute, Palo Alto is looking to offer users a technology platform to help customers securely train and deploy open-weight models as they expand their use of AI.
Open-weight models, AI systems whose trained settings are publicly released, present security challenges, including the risk of model tampering, data leakage and misuse by bad actors.

"Applied Compute extends Palo Alto's push beyond traditional cybersecurity into enterprise AI. The opportunity is to bring AI infrastructure and security closer together," said Shaul Eyal, analyst at TD Cowen.
The deal is expected to close in the third quarter of fiscal 2027.
Palo Alto now expects fiscal 2027 revenue to be between $14.52 billion and $14.57 billion, compared with its prior expectation of $14.10 billion to $14.20 billion.
Its first-quarter revenue came in at $3.45 billion, up 39 per cent from a year earlier, beating estimates of $3.31 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.

paragraphs: CHICAGO, Nov 18 (Reuters) - The state of Arizona has opened a criminal investigation into OpenAI and other AI companies relating to the "apparent infiltration of banks by rogue AI agents," Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes said Wednesday.
A criminal investigation does not necessarily mean charges will be brought. Mayes said her office was investigating whether Arizona state law was being violated on an ongoing basis.
"The state of Arizona is very worried about this, and we are looking at it from multiple angles," Mayes told a press conference in Chicago.
Mayes declined to identify the other companies her office was investigating. She said her office had been in contact with Arizona banks, but declined to name them or give their responses.
A spokesperson for OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The banking industry has become increasingly concerned that sophisticated AI agents could harm the banking system and the institutions trusted to hold people's wealth. Reuters reported last month that major US banks have been blocking third-party AI agents from operating inside customer accounts and making transactions.

Mayes' comments come two days after California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI for allegedly developing a dangerous product without adequate safety procedures or oversight after reports that its AI models had carried out cyberattacks independently.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on that lawsuit, but the company has acknowledged a general need for more transparency around rogue AI behavior and said it was reinforcing its safeguards. On September 16, the company published a new framework for disclosing such incidents, saying it would err on the side of transparency "even when significance is uncertain."

paragraphs: NEW YORK, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Meta’s AI agent Muse, embodied by a smiley, fuzzy mascot named Jolly, has burrowed into encrypted personal messages, supplied made-up information about purchases and sent users chats seemingly meant for other people, a fraught start for a bot meant to simplify life for consumers, according to internal company posts reviewed by Reuters.

The unbidden actions by Muse – one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads since its September launch, and the centerpiece of Meta’s plan to generate billions of dollars in AI revenue – have prompted unnerved employees to raise concerns it could be mixing up conversations between different accounts and exposing users’ private data, the posts showed.

In some of those cases, Meta staffers reported the agent sending them messages about a childcare request they had not made, career advice they had not sought, product orders they had not placed and bank account balances that were not theirs.

In one post, from earlier this month, an employee told colleagues his Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
“I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse. I’m afraid it’s sending other’s bank info to me,” the staffer wrote in his post.

In another example, an employee using Muse on her personal phone reported it had surprised her with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, an end-to-end encrypted messaging service popular with privacy advocates that competes with Meta’s WhatsApp.
“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee said in her post.

A colleague responded, saying he had discovered Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on phones with Google’s Android operating system after being similarly caught off guard by unsolicited chats related to apps he had not connected.

For this story, Reuters reviewed more than two dozen internal posts describing undesired actions by Muse since its debut, many of them from a feedback group where Meta employees flag problems to the team building the agent. Reuters also worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute, a non-profit that studies AI’s impact on society, to replicate Muse’s access to Signal messages. The results of those tests indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others.

In response to questions about Signal access and other Muse safety concerns, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts described the Reuters examples as “isolated incidents,” saying the company prioritizes safety, conducts extensive internal testing and continuously updates products to improve protections.

Muse needs to see and interact with people’s computers in order to work on their behalf, and can access other apps only via permissions they explicitly grant, Roberts said. He said many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations, a term referring to AI models’ tendency to make things up, and had already been addressed.
Reuters was unable to establish whether Muse was giving users other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information.

The Muse incidents highlight the risks associated with an emerging category of consumer AI agents hitting the market from Meta, OpenAI and others, pitched as the next big wave of AI technology. The bots promise to reshape how digital exchanges operate by executing time-saving tasks like answering emails, booking appointments and making online purchases without direct instructions.

Meta is ahead of competitors so far, with Muse consistently topping app download charts after heavy promotion to the company’s more than 3.6 billion users on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. The app’s retention rate is also strong, with around a quarter of the people who have set up Muse accounts returning to use it each day, the company has disclosed.

To work effectively, agents need deep access to smartphones and computers. However, they are also prone to making mistakes, exploiting obscure loopholes and accomplishing their objectives in sometimes harmful ways. OpenAI and Anthropic, for instance, have revealed instances of their AI agents unexpectedly hacking other companies and weakening systems designed to monitor their activities.

Some banks and retailers have responded to those risks by blocking agents. The technology is also posing new challenges for operating system providers like Apple and Google, which manage the permissions agents use to navigate around people’s devices. Apple, for instance, changed its operating system this week to give people more control over agents’ data usage after an Inc. Magazine columnist accused Muse of reading private chats from the Messages app on his Mac.

Meta has assured Muse users it isolates each agent in its own secure “virtual machine” – a cloud-based emulation of a personal computer – and gives people full control over which apps they connect. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has cited those protections in dismissing calls for industry-wide AI safety standards, arguing companies already have incentives to build safe products, both to earn consumers’ trust and avoid legal risks. Even so, Meta warns incoming users Muse may make mistakes and its terms of service hold users responsible for the agent’s actions.

To find out how Muse might access encrypted messages without users’ knowledge, Reuters provided a description of the Meta employee’s post – where the bot randomly prompted her to respond to a Signal message – to staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute. Reuters then worked with them to replicate the access she had observed.

Testers prompted Muse to read Signal messages on different operating systems. On an Android phone and an Apple laptop, it responded by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead using permissions granted during the bot’s initial setup to pull in the message text, leveraging those authorizations in ways a user might not anticipate.

Specifically, on Android, it used its permission to access the device's push notifications to retrieve the messages, just as the Meta employees had described. On Apple’s macOS, it used a combination of the computer’s accessibility and screenshot tools, repurposing settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers.
The same requests were blocked in tests conducted on an iPhone.
The results indicate Meta is interpreting the permissions granted by Muse users broadly, an approach that has long earned the company criticism from privacy advocates and hefty fines from regulators.

In response to Reuters’ findings, Signal President Meredith Whittaker accused Meta of launching Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity,” calling the deployment of agents that can gain wide access to people’s devices “technologically reckless.”

She called for app developers like Signal to be given “consistent technical ways” to mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents, for Meta and other AI companies to honor those boundaries and for operating system providers to enforce the rules.

Presented with the same findings, Apple and Google said they were considering changes to give people more control over what they authorize with AI agents – though Google, like Meta, noted that people already “must deliberately grant permissions” for apps to access Android notifications.

Apple said it had built its accessibility tools for people with disabilities and cautioned that leveraging them “for unintended purposes” could put people’s personal information at risk. Its operating system update this week effectively closed the pathway identified by Reuters, sharply restricting developers’ use of accessibility tools on Macs and introducing a new agent-oriented set of permissions.
“We are committed to ensuring users understand exactly what they are allowing, so they can make informed choices about their data and privacy,” Apple said in a statement.

In other cases discussed internally, staffers reported cases of Muse informing users about transactions that never occurred and making up prices on products they did purchase, costing them real money. In one incident, the agent booked a non-refundable Airbnb stay without permission, an employee reported.

Some of the incidents that raised the most concern involved cryptic out-of-context messages sent by the agent that appeared to contain other people’s information, in many cases phrased as replies to queries the users had never submitted.

In a late September social media post, a member of Meta’s Superintelligence team behind Muse initially described a user report of a similar problem as a temporary hallucination-related glitch, resolved the same day it arose. However, the internal posts reviewed by Reuters showed such incidents occurring as far back as mid-September and continuing through this month.
In one such post, an employee reported his Muse sending him a message “out of nowhere” saying it was unable to submit a request related to a parent’s control over who could access their child’s data.
He had done nothing to trigger the chat, and had never discussed child data or caregiving access with his Muse, he said.
When he asked Muse about the message, the bot replied: “I don’t have a good explanation for it other than that it wasn’t related to our conversation. Let’s ignore it. How can I help?”

Another staffer said Muse randomly offered to “message the seller” about picking up a coffee table. When the employee asked Muse, “What are you talking about?” the agent responded that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.”
This was “not my conversation,” the employee said in his post, expressing concern about a “possible cross-account context leak.”

To address employee worries, another Superintelligence team member told the internal feedback group in early November that the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with users in between sessions.

“These (hallucinations) unfortunately bias towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks,” he said, adding that he was aware of several other cases involving “crypto-related things too, like giving people updates on their Bitcoin balances.”
He said the issues involved both the underlying AI model and the software enabling Muse to take actions, and that the team was working through them.
Roberts declined to answer Reuters questions about those issues, including how many there were and why they were persisting.

paragraphs: Korea surpassed $1 trillion in annual exports for the first time Thursday, reaching the milestone at 2:09:38 p.m. as global AI investment boosted demand for semiconductors. It became the fourth country to reach the mark, after the United States, Germany and China. The government projects exports will total about $1.17 trillion this year, but officials warned that AI investment slowdowns, chip-price volatility and trade barriers could threaten momentum.
Containers are stacked at a port in Incheon, Tuesday. Yonhap

Korea has surpassed $1 trillion in annual exports for the first time in its history, becoming the world's fourth country to reach the milestone after the United States, Germany and China, as a global artificial intelligence (AI) boom drives demand for semiconductors.
The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources announced Thursday that the country's cumulative exports reached the $1 trillion mark at 2:09:38 p.m.
The achievement comes 19 years after China reached the milestone in 2007, following the U.S. and Germany in 2006.
The government projects annual exports will reach approximately $1.17 trillion this year, following last year's record of $709.3 billion.

The ministry explained global technology companies’ expanding AI investments were the biggest driver of export growth, boosting demand for semiconductors and computers while pushing up memory chip prices.
Semiconductor exports reached $396.8 billion in the January-October period, almost triple the $135.4 billion recorded in 2025, as the price of memory chips, including DRAM and NAND, climbed.
Demand for AI data center infrastructure has also boosted exports of computers, electrical equipment and nonferrous metals, including storage devices, transformers, power cables, copper and aluminum.

Higher international oil prices, driven by uncertainty over supplies from the Middle East and Russian export restrictions, lifted the value of petroleum product exports despite limits on gasoline and diesel shipments.
The average export price of petroleum products rose 62 percent to $1,105 per ton in the January-October period from $681 a year earlier.

Other export industries, including shipbuilding and displays, also performed well, while cosmetics, pharmaceuticals and agricultural and seafood products posted record performances. Cosmetics exports alone reached $12.4 billion in the first 10 months, surpassing their previous full-year record of $11.4 billion.

Overall, 16 of 20 major export categories expanded year-on-year, with eight recording their strongest January-October performance ever. Exports excluding semiconductors rose 20 percent in the first 10 months, underscoring growth beyond the chip boom. Seven of the country's nine major export markets also recorded growth.

“This is a valuable achievement made possible by Korean companies competing in global markets, businesspeople and workers putting in long hours on the production floor and everyone who has contributed to the country's export efforts,” Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said.

“We will not rest on this year's $1 trillion export milestone and will seek new sources of growth to sustain the momentum, while working to ensure that strong exports translate into stronger regional economies and more jobs for young people.”

Kang Gam-chan, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy's director general for trade and investment, speaks during a briefing at Government Complex Sejong, Wednesday. Courtesy of Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources

However, sustaining the current level of exports will depend on how the country navigates risks, including a potential slowdown in AI investment, semiconductor price volatility, lower oil prices and Chinese oversupply, as well as growing trade barriers in major markets.

The ministry also noted that the benefits of export growth may be less visible to the public because semiconductors, petrochemicals and petroleum products generate fewer jobs than shipbuilding and automobile manufacturing.

“Unlike the shipbuilding and auto industries, which have long supply chains and generate substantial employment, semiconductors, petrochemicals and petroleum products are relatively less labor-intensive, so the benefits of export growth may be less noticeable to the general public,” Kang Gam-chan, the ministry’s director general for trade and investment, said during a briefing on Wednesday at Government Complex Sejong.

He warned that large trade surpluses could invite further pressure from trading partners, particularly the U.S., and called for stronger investment-based economic partnerships. While Japan's overseas investment offered a point of reference, he said Korea should maintain its domestic manufacturing capabilities while expanding production overseas.

“We should not simply follow Japan's path. We need to maintain a substantial domestic production base, including advanced plants and mother factories for research and core production, while also expanding our manufacturing capacity overseas,” he said.

paragraphs: Nov 19 (Reuters) - Anthropic's record $81 billion IPO brings to Wall Street an avatar of a sector that proponents herald as an economic panacea, while detractors warn it has stoked a market bubble and could ultimately threaten humanity itself.

More immediately, the Claude chatbot maker's debut after securing a $1.5 trillion valuation in the IPO, together with Tuesday's earnings report by AI poster child Nvidia, signals the industry has nominally passed the two big tests facing it this week.

The strong demand for Anthropic shares amid a broader tech selloff offers hope to the sector, even as a rocky market reception for Nvidia results which looked strong at first blush, signals the euphoria around the sector has cooled.

"I've looked at this whole week as a referendum on AI. Nvidia gave us a read on the buildout, and Anthropic is about to give us a read on investor appetite for the next generation of AI companies," Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion, said before the Anthropic debut.
AI technology has boosted economic growth, sparked doomsday warnings and arguably helped usher in a data-center-skeptic Democratic tsunami in the US midterm elections.

Investors who once embraced the boom have turned skeptical in recent weeks over concerns that the enormous spending needed to build out the sector and the incipient crushing debt loads may not be justified by the eventual returns.
An extramarital-affair scandal involving Nvidia's CEO and a spike in Treasury yields have further unnerved investors.
As the first frontier AI company to go public, Anthropic is poised to become the sector's benchmark, with its arch-rival OpenAI reportedly eyeing a 2027 listing.

The company sold 980 million shares at $83 each, pricing the IPO above its initial range of $70 to $78 set when it launched the roadshow. The additional $26 billion raised through a private placement takes the total haul to over $107 billion.

"Some of the demand may simply reflect investors not wanting to miss out on the rare opportunity to gain exposure to a leading AI company, even if its long-term profitability remains uncertain," IPOX associate Lukas Muehlbauer said.
London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates passive demand from index-tracking funds will account for about 28% of Anthropic's shares offered, or roughly $19 billion.
When it debuts on the Nasdaq later on Thursday, Anthropic will join the world's trillion-dollar club, alongside technology giants such as Microsoft, Apple and Nvidia.
The listing will also give retail investors a chance to pile into one of the AI industry's hottest names, potentially amplifying swings in the stock as trading begins.
The buzz has already spilled onto prediction markets, where traders are placing bets on everything from its opening pop to where the stock will close on its first day.

Debate has intensified across global markets in recent months over whether the AI boom is veering into bubble territory, with economists, some of the world's biggest CEOs, and political leaders split over its sustainability.

Much of the scrutiny has focused on circular financing arrangements. A complicated web of deals between AI companies, chipmakers, cloud providers and investors has raised questions over how much of the industry's growth is being fueled by money circulating within the same ecosystem.
Anthropic's breakneck growth has so far defied these concerns, but some investors have said they may wait for the initial euphoria to subside before buying.
"It doesn't have to be a bad company for it to be a bad investment at the IPO price," said Nic Puckrin, cross-asset analyst and founder of Coin Bureau.

Anthropic has nearly $900 billion in computing commitments with partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google, underscoring how its rapid growth hinges on securing vast amounts of future computing capacity, some of which relies on financing beyond the company's control.

Investors will be watching Anthropic's debut and subsequent trading closely, with analysts expecting the stock to emerge as a proxy for the broader AI trade as questions over valuations, spending and returns weigh on sentiment.

The company will also need to balance growth with calls to slow the development of advanced AI models over concerns that they pose cybersecurity threats and could be exploited by bad actors to target critical government and private infrastructure.
Anthropic warned in its IPO prospectus that AI could behave unpredictably and advance faster than oversight mechanisms, posing potentially "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."

paragraphs: Menlo Ventures and Spark Capital are two such firms emerging with some of the biggest returns by multiple
FOR decades, venture capital thrived on small bets that became billion-dollar companies.
Then came Anthropic, rewriting the playbook and forcing investors to write fatter checks to buy stakes at unheard-of valuations.

The artificial intelligence lab’s shares began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday (Nov 19) at a US$1.5 trillion valuation, delivering multibillion-dollar windfalls to venture investors at a moment when the industry needs fresh liquidity to fund more bets on AI companies.
The stock closed at US$97.17, up 17 per cent from its initial public offering price of US$83.
Anthropic’s stock market value ended the day at about US$1.3 trillion, based on its outstanding shares, or US$1.8 trillion, based on its fully diluted shares.
To join the fundraising frenzy, especially at later stages, venture capital firms invested billions, tapping their own investors for additional capital through special-purpose vehicles.

Menlo Ventures and Spark Capital emerged with some of the biggest returns by multiple.

Spark Capital was the first venture capital firm to lead an Anthropic investment, in a US$450 million Series C round in 2023 at a valuation of US$4.5 billion. Spark general partner Yasmin Razavi, who spearheaded the investment, remains the only investor who sits on Anthropic’s board.

Writing the largest check in the firm’s history, early-stage firm Menlo invested over US$1 billion for a stake of nearly 1.5 per cent, according to a person familiar with the investment. At a US$1.5 trillion market cap, Menlo’s stake is worth over US$20 billion.

To invest beyond the capacity of its existing fund, Menlo raised a US$750 million special-purpose vehicle from limited partners, a tactic that became increasingly common as funding rounds grew, given the capital needs of AI companies.
Sequoia Capital, long known for its early bets, joined a later round and still stands to earn billions of dollars.

Sequoia passed on Anthropic at lower prices. After a leadership change, it wrote its first check at the start of this year, joining a round led by Singapore’s GIC and Coatue at a US$380 billion post-money valuation in February.

It later co-led, alongside Altimeter, Dragoneer and Greenoaks, a round at US$965 billion. Sequoia has invested US$3 billion in Anthropic and continued to invest more through Anthropic’s IPO, signalling further conviction in the AI lab.

Lightspeed Venture Partners, which invested more than US$3 billion in Anthropic, now holds over 2 per cent of the company, making it the largest financial investor in the company, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The returns are possible because of the rapid rise in Anthropic’s valuation and revenue. Its annualised revenue grew from about US$1 billion at the start of 2025 to about US$81 billion last month, as its valuation climbed from US$61.5 billion in March 2025 to US$965 billion in the latest private round this May.
Strategic backers, too, supply much of the unprecedented capital and computing power needed by AI labs. The combined stake of Amazon and Alphabet’s Google in Anthropic is about 28.4 per cent.

Will Griffith, a partner at Iconiq, said: “We’re living through a very unique time of profound change happening at a higher velocity than ever before. The scale of the impact of these businesses and the breadth of market opportunities is larger than anything we’ve seen before.
“And that is going to afford investment opportunities that are larger than what we’ve seen in the past.”
He has invested US$6.1 billion, making the fund the second-largest financial investor by ownership in Anthropic. REUTERS

paragraphs: WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross was "fired" from his job, a person close to the White House said on Thursday, days after technology outages disrupted US air travel, banking and national security systems.

The ouster comes as US President Donald Trump and his administration face mounting scrutiny over their response to the series of disruptions over the past week, including a global outage affecting hundreds of millions of Microsoft users and a nationwide halt to air travel that disrupted more than 18,000 flights.
The dismissal of Cairncross dismissal is the administration's first major personnel move since the outages.

Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source.
"The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position," said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Cairncross said in a statement on Thursday night it was the "honor of a lifetime to serve" in Trump's administration.

The recent technology disruptions are likely linked to corporate efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered software vulnerabilities in the AI age, cybersecurity experts told Reuters. Advanced AI tools make it easier for companies to uncover weaknesses in their cybersecurity protections.
The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday the disruptions were separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.

Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri on Tuesday told reporters in Washington the Trump administration should brief lawmakers on the outages so they can "share with the American people what's happening here."

Cairncross was an executive at the Republican National Committee before assuming the cyber director role. His successor will need to be confirmed by the US Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.
