paragraphs: Secure messaging service Signal said it will restrict the screenshot function on smartphones to prevent AI agents from reading private conversations. In a blog post published on the 20th (local time), Signal pointed out that AI features built directly into operating systems (OS) are accessing device data in ways app developers cannot control, and demanded that platform operators such as Apple, Google and Microsoft provide concrete blocking tools.

Signal itself acknowledged that the measure is not complete. "The current wave of agentic AI integration is creating an environment that is increasingly hostile to privacy," the company said, calling it "an existential threat to Signal and our ability to uphold our mission." It added that "operating systems govern the very environment in which apps like Signal must exist."

The biggest concern is AI that is deeply integrated into the OS, such as Apple's Siri AI or Google's Gemini Intelligence. According to Signal, these agents can read what is displayed on screen and act on the user's behalf based on that, meaning that Signal messages protected by end-to-end encryption can be pulled outside the encrypted environment. The company noted that the moment AI scans the screen, Signal's security environment is neutralized.

With this measure, Signal will introduce a setting that blocks screenshot access on users' devices and turn it on by default. When Signal detects a screenshot attempt or an AI assistant's screen access, it displays a pop-up window that lets users lift the block depending on the device type. Signal also blocked Microsoft's Recall AI from taking screenshots on Windows last year. However, it said such protections are difficult to provide reliably on Apple's macOS.

Signal's concerns are backed by a recently confirmed real-world case. It was confirmed that Meta's AI agent Muse bypassed official integration tools to access Signal messages on Apple computers and Google Android smartphones. Muse used the broad OS-level permissions granted during the app's initial setup to pull messages in ways users did not expect. On Apple's macOS, it combined accessibility tools with the screenshot function to capture Signal conversations, extract text from the images and reproduce it inside the Muse app.

Meta countered that an agent must be able to see and interact with the computer to act on the user's behalf, and that Muse accesses other apps only through permissions the user has explicitly granted. Apple blocked that path with an OS update released this week, but at the same time introduced a new permission system aimed at agents that allows similar functions with additional warnings.

Signal urged that app developers be given a clear way to fully exclude their apps from AI assistants' data processing, including screen reading, notifications and file system access. Signal, which is run by a nonprofit foundation, has minimized the data it stores on servers, excluded advertising and provided end-to-end encryption. The company's judgment is that these protections are neutralized the moment AI scans the screen.

The issue comes as Apple accelerates development of its own AI agent. In a recent job posting, Apple disclosed plans to develop a general-purpose AI agent that handles a computer like a human, performing web searches, coding, app control and coordination of multiple sub-agents. It is considering a launch as early as the end of next year, but development is still at an early stage. Apple CEO John Ternus is said to have urged Craig Federighi, senior vice president of software engineering, to push the AI strategy faster and more boldly.

The competitive landscape is also heating up quickly. Meta's Muse ranked second among free apps on Apple's App Store with restaurant and travel booking and news briefing features, while OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude also placed in the top five. Anthropic has expanded user testing of its own agent Duet, OpenAI has added features to Dots, and Google overhauled its agent tasks this week. After news of Apple's AI agent development emerged, Meta shares fell about 2% and Anthropic more than 3% in after-hours trading.

The market expects tensions between platform operators and privacy apps to intensify further. The fact that platforms can control the paths through which OS-integrated AI accesses other apps' data shows that competitiveness in the AI agent era depends not only on model performance but also on the design of access permissions at the operating system level. Apple has already been sued by the US Department of Justice, including over allegations that it blocked rivals' access to features and hardware, so attention is focused on how Signal's demands will be reflected. Signal assessed that in Apple's upcoming iOS 27.3, Siri will be able to call a car or book a restaurant through external apps, but that this is far from a full agent that moves across multiple apps and handles complex tasks on its own.

China’s securities regulator has told some law firms it will not approve plans by red-chip companies to list outside mainland China, people familiar with the matter said. The move marks a further tightening of China’s controls on offshore fundraising and will deal a blow to Hong Kong’s initial public offering (IPO) market.
Red-chip companies are incorporated outside China and legally classified as foreign companies, but hold assets and operate businesses within China through equity holdings or contractual arrangements.

Reuters reported on Friday (20 November), citing people familiar with the matter, that the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) recently told representatives of law firms that red-chip companies established after new offshore listing rules took effect in 2023 must move their place of incorporation back to China before they can list.

In March 2023, the CSRC introduced new filing rules for overseas securities offerings and listings by domestic companies, bringing both direct and indirect overseas listings under a filing-based regulatory framework.
Before that, Chinese companies did not need regulatory approval to raise funds overseas through offshore holding structures.
In March this year, the CSRC told Reuters it was reviewing the “necessity and compliance” of red-chip structures.

However, despite warnings from the authorities, some red-chip companies seeking IPOs and their advisers continued to seek regulatory approval, hoping to list outside mainland China without dismantling their existing structures or moving their place of incorporation back to China, according to one of the people familiar with the matter.
The person added that most applicants had failed to convince Chinese regulators that their red-chip structures were necessary, prompting the regulators to take a tougher stance.

US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed that humans should always be involved in military decisions made by artificial intelligence, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday.

“I think it was very important that the President Trump, and President Xi agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions,” Bessent told CNBC, using the term “SI,” or superintelligence, for the technology.
Bessent said there was also “very robust discussion on what can be done in terms of containing the growth of nuclear weapons.”
He said the leaders held “a robust discussion on trade policy, AI,” and discussed the Russia-Ukraine war with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump, Xi and Putin met Thursday in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. In a joint declaration after the meeting, the three leaders reaffirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.”

paragraphs: NEW YORK/WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The US Securities and Exchange Commission is probing Nvidia's accounting practices, said two people briefed on the matter, adding to the legal woes facing the scandal-hit chip giant.

The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday reported that the SEC was probing Nvidia but said it could not ascertain the focus of the investigation. The people, who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential issues, said SEC enforcement staff are scrutinizing potential accounting issues at the company.
A spokesperson for the SEC declined to comment. Spokespeople for Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Reuters could not immediately determine when the SEC opened its inquiry or exactly what potential accounting issues the watchdog is examining. Investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and many close without resulting in enforcement action.

Still, the accounting focus of the probe, which Reuters is reporting for the first time, increases pressure on Nvidia, whose investors are still reeling from revelations about ousted CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital relationships, including with Alice Huang, who US authorities suspect is a Chinese spy. China has denied she is a spy.

Alice Huang led Singapore-based Megaspeed, historically a large Nvidia chip customer, people familiar with the matter have said. US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over possible violations of export controls related to alleged shipments of Nvidia AI chips to China, the US Justice and Commerce departments said this week.
The crisis has sent shares in Nvidia, a linchpin of the AI boom, tumbling more than a third and stoked calls in Washington for tougher action on tech threats posed by Beijing.

Megaspeed has said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and that it conducted "lawful business." Reuters has not been able to reach Alice Huang. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair in a November 8 statement following the reports of his relationship with Alice Huang, without referring to her by name.

The SEC probe is the latest of Nvidia's legal woes. The Justice Department has also been reviewing Nvidia's $12.9-billion deal to buy open-source platform Hugging Face alongside a broader antitrust investigation into the company's acquisitions and practices, Reuters reported last month.
SINGAPORE ACCOUNTING CHANGE BACK IN FOCUS

Last year, Nvidia changed how it reports geographic revenue, using customer headquarters rather than billing addresses, which it said would better reflect the geographic profile of its revenue. The change resulted in Singapore being removed from its geographical breakdown.
The Financial Times, citing company accounts, reported on Tuesday that Nvidia had made the change even as Singapore sales soared to almost half its global revenue.
That accounting shift has drawn renewed press scrutiny in the wake of the Alice Huang scandal.
Southeast Asia has become a hub for chip smuggling to China since the Biden administration barred advanced AI chip exports to that country over concerns they could boost Beijing’s military.

Analysts and investors have also grown increasingly concerned about circular AI financing deals, in which chipmakers including Nvidia have pursued complex financial arrangements to help customers fund purchases of their chips and the construction of costly AI infrastructure, such as data centers. Nvidia has backed AI companies and cloud providers and provided guarantees connected to data-center projects that use its equipment.

Critics say such arrangements can make it harder for investors to assess the quality of chipmakers' revenue and their true financial exposure. Speaking to Reuters last month, SEC enforcement chief David Woodcock said the agency was examining AI companies' corporate disclosures to ensure issuers are giving investors the full picture on potential risks.

On its Tuesday earnings call, Nvidia's interim CEO and former CFO Colette Kress said the company was proud of its role in supporting the AI industry, but would be far more selective moving forward about AI industry financing deals.

The SEC under President Donald Trump has pulled back on enforcement, saying it will focus on bread-and-butter securities fraud, including accounting violations that have long been a mainstay of its enforcement work. It recently launched a new financial reporting and accounting unit within its enforcement division, aimed at developing cases in accounting and auditing areas.

paragraphs: Business Recorder • 22 Nov 2026, 5:00 PM PKT • 1 min read

Business Recorder reported that Anthropic’s IPO, which took place on Thursday, raised more than half a billion dollars in underwriting fees but drew complaints from some bankers about the way it was run. The offering surpassed SpaceX’s June listing, and bankers cited a compressed timetable, late changes, delayed financial projections and rushed approvals. The companies aim to strengthen BILL's financial operations platform and expand its capabilities for small and midsize businesses.
